title: The Kem Kem rivers
summary: The head of a vast river system in what is now south-east Morocco, about 100–95 million years ago: wide braided channels and sandbanks, giant fish, and more big meat-eating dinosaurs than anywhere on Earth today.

place.says: The rocks are in south-east Morocco, along the escarpment called the Kem Kem, by the border with Algeria.
place.why: Where the fossils are found today.

place.says: About 100–95 million years ago, in the early Late Cretaceous (the Cenomanian).
place.why: The site’s review dates the Kem Kem Group to the Cenomanian.

place.says: Then this place lay at about 21° north — some 10° nearer the equator than today — near the northern edge of Africa, with the Tethys Sea to the north.
place.why: The atlas carries the site back on its plate with the plate model of Merdith et al. (2021); another model would place it a little differently.

landscape.says: A vast river system flowing north to a delta on the Tethys Sea, in wide channels around big sandbanks that moved with every flood.
landscape.why: River sandstones and pebble beds; the current marks in them show the water flowed north.
landscape.picture: a broad, shallow, slow river, brownish-green, braided around a pale sandbank island

landscape.says: Low banks of sand and reddish sandstone, with bars of gravel the rivers dropped where they slowed.
landscape.why: The rock itself: the Gara Sbaa and Douira formations.
landscape.picture: a low, level far bank of pale sand and reddish sandstone; a wide, flat near shore of sand and small pebbles

landscape.why: Fish and rays of a kind that live in both, such as the sawfish Onchopristis.

landscape.says: A hot climate with harsh seasons and dry spells.
landscape.why: From the rocks and fossils, in the site’s review; it fits the latitude the plates give the site.

landscape.says: Tall conifers, probably related to monkey-puzzle trees.
landscape.why: Pieces of petrified wood, probably from such conifers, are most of what is known of the plants here; how many trees stood on the banks is not known.
landscape.picture: a few tall conifers related to monkey-puzzle trees (straight bare trunks, branches in tiers near the top) spaced along the far bank, and drift logs in the water

landscape.says: Low leafy plants at the water’s edge.
landscape.why: Leaves of flowering plants and others come from an old pond at Oum Tkout; their exact kinds and where they grew along the rivers are not known.
landscape.picture: low leafy shrubs and small plants at the water’s edge; a few ferns

landscape.says: No grass, no palms, no broadleaf forest, no flowers in bloom; no cliffs, mountains or volcanoes.
landscape.why: None is recorded in the Kem Kem rocks; grasslands came many millions of years later, and the land was a low river plain.
landscape.not: grass or grassland, palm trees, cycads, broadleaf forest, flowers in bloom, cliffs, mountains, volcanoes

landscape.says: A hot, hazy afternoon in the dry season.
landscape.why: The time of day and the weather are the painter’s; they fit the climate, but no rock records an afternoon.
landscape.picture: a hot, hazy dry-season afternoon under a pale sky

life.says: These animals are found in the same rocks — but their bones are river-worn and mixed together, so whether they all lived side by side at one moment is not known.
life.why: Most fossils here are single bones and teeth rolled along by the rivers. It is part of “Stromer’s riddle”: why so many big meat-eaters and so few plant-eaters? Perhaps many hunted the rivers’ giant fish; perhaps the rivers mixed bones from different times.

life.says: Spinosaurus, a long, low hunter with a sail on its back and a paddle-like tail.
life.why: A partial skeleton and a tail from the Kem Kem.
life.alternatives: Others read it as a wader that hunted from the shallows rather than a swimmer (Hone & Holtz 2021; Sereno et al. 2022).
life.picture: Spinosaurus at the water’s edge: a long, low theropod with short hind legs, a long narrow crocodile-like snout, a tall sail, and a deep paddle-like tail

life.says: Carcharodontosaurus, a giant meat-eater with a long, deep skull and blade-like teeth.
life.why: Its skull and partial bones are from these rocks; the rest of the body is rebuilt from its close relatives, which is inferred.
life.picture: a giant two-legged meat-eater with a long, deep skull, short three-fingered arms and a long tail held level, on the far bank

life.why: One partial skeleton from these rocks; its skull is not known, so its head is a guess from its likely relatives.
life.alternatives: It has been placed among the coelurosaurs and, more often since, among the ceratosaurs; the reconstruction changes with the placement.
life.picture: a slender, long-legged meat-eater with a long tail held level, beside the larger one

life.says: Big pterosaurs — Alanqa and Siroccopteryx — overhead.
life.why: Known from jaws, snouts and neck bones found here; their bodies are rebuilt from relatives, which is inferred.
life.picture: two long-jawed, long-necked pterosaurs flying high over the river

life.says: Giant fish: the sawfish-like Onchopristis, a coelacanth, a lungfish and a gar — and the long-snouted crocodile relative Elosuchus.
life.why: Onchopristis teeth are the commonest fossil here; the others are known from bones and skulls.
life.picture: dark shapes of large fish under the water

life.says: Also here, but not in this painting: an abelisaurid meat-eater, the long-necked plant-eater Rebbachisaurus, side-necked turtles.
life.why: Bones from these rocks; left out of this picture to keep it to one moment by the river.

moment.says: An ordinary hot afternoon on the river: Spinosaurus at the water’s edge, two big meat-eaters on the far bank, pterosaurs overhead. Nothing in particular is happening — and that is the point: no place on Earth today has so many big hunters.
moment.why: The gathering is invented: no fossil records these animals at this spot at this moment. It is chosen to show what is unusual about the Kem Kem, its many big meat-eaters.

moment.says: Spinosaurus is shown at the water’s edge.
moment.why: Both readings of its life — a swimmer and a wader — allow it there.

discovery.says: In 1954 René Lavocat named the long-necked Rebbachisaurus garasbae from bones found here.
discovery.why: Its name and author, re-described in 2015.

discovery.says: In 2010 a big pterosaur, Alanqa, was named from jaws found in these rocks.
In 2014 a new partial skeleton from the Kem Kem changed the picture of Spinosaurus: short hind legs, an animal at home in water. In 2020 its tail, found here, was described as a paddle.

In 2021 and 2022 the question split: some argued Spinosaurus waded and hunted from the shallows rather than swam (Hone & Holtz; Sereno and others), while a study of its dense bones argued it dived (Fabbri and others). It is still open.
In 2020 a review gathered the geology and all the fossils of the Kem Kem Group.
